name: Sea buckthorn oil

card.summary: A carotenoid-rich orange oil from Hippophae berries and seeds, used in creams and supplements, with small human trials but little skin-specific evidence.
card.note: Studies on skin aging exist as registrations but published human skin results were not found among the sources.

quick.overview:
Sea buckthorn oil is taken from the berry pulp and seeds of Hippophae rhamnoides, a hardy shrub of Europe and Asia. The pulp oil is orange to deep red, rich in carotenoids and palmitoleic acid, while the seed oil is richer in linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid.

It is added to creams, lotions and supplements and is promoted for skin repair and anti-aging. Published human studies cover dry eye and other mucosal conditions; a skin-aging trial was registered, but no published human skin results were found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents attribute its effects to carotenoids, vitamin E, sterols and unsaturated fatty acids with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. Laboratory work on human skin cells found that seed oil altered lipid metabolism changes induced by UV exposure.
quick.risks: Reviews describe the oil as generally well tolerated in the trials cited, but safety data specific to cosmetic use are limited. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient and food supplement; regulatory status varies by country.

lead: Sea buckthorn oil is a golden-orange to red oil obtained from the berries, seeds and sometimes leaves of the shrub Hippophae rhamnoides (now also classed as Elaeagnus rhamnoides), native to cold-temperate Europe and Asia.[1][2][7] It is used in creams, lotions, hair products and dietary supplements, where it is marketed for skin repair, hydration, a healthier-looking complexion and anti-aging.[2][7]

Pulp oil and seed oil differ in composition: pulp oil is rich in palmitoleic acid and carotenoids, whereas seed oil is richer in linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids.[3][4] Its carotenoids, tocopherols and sterols are the basis for its use in skincare, and a laboratory study found seed oil modified UV-induced changes in lipid metabolism in cultured human skin cells.[1][11]

Human trials of the oil have mostly examined oral use for dry eye and mucosal dryness; one trial of oral and topical use on skin aging was registered in 2008.[5][6][14] Reviews describe much of the other evidence as preclinical.[4]

paras: Sea buckthorn is a spiny, deciduous, suckering shrub of the family Elaeagnaceae that grows 2 to 5 m tall and bears bright orange berries 6 to 8 mm across.[7] It is native across cold-temperate Eurasia, from the North Sea and Baltic coasts to the Himalayas and northern China, and about 3.0 million hectares exist worldwide, mostly in China.[7] The genus name combines Greek words for horse and light, reflecting the ancient practice of feeding the leaves to horses to brighten their coats.[7] The berries contain about 400 mg of vitamin C per 100 g, plus vitamins E and K and several carotenoids.[7]

Reviews describe the oil as containing a wide range of active compounds including carotenoids, tocopherols, sterols, and polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fatty acids.[3][4] Reference sources report pulp oil at roughly 1.5 to 3 percent of the fruit and seed oil near 11 percent of seed weight, with beta-carotene the main carotenoid.[7] The fatty acid profile of developing berries and the mature seed has been characterised in detail,[8] and the oil has been compared with other unconventional plant oils for cosmetic use.[9] Its xanthophylls have been studied for bioaccessibility.[10] Wikipedia notes that the pomace left after pressing can be used to yield oil or a yellow-orange food colouring.[7]

Sea buckthorn oil is incorporated into hand creams, shampoos, massage oils and moisturisers.[7] Marketing and reference accounts credit it with moisturising, soothing and anti-aging effects; the Grokipedia entry additionally describes wound- and burn-healing claims, which that source attributes to reviews.[2] Laboratory work found that seed oil modified UV-induced changes in lipid metabolism in cultured human skin cells.[11]

Accounts describe use of the fruit and oil in Tibetan, Chinese, Mongolian and Russian traditional medicine for wounds, burns and digestive complaints.[2] The oil is also used as a food colourant and supplement.[2] Reviews have discussed possible health effects of its fatty acids and compounds, including cardiovascular and anticancer research, much of it preclinical.[4][12][13]

Sea buckthorn oil appears in hand creams, shampoos, massage oils and moisturisers.[7] Proponents point to palmitoleic acid and carotenoids as reasons it is used for dry or irritated skin. Reviews of its fatty acids discuss effects on human health in general terms.[3] A cosmetics-oriented comparison of unconventional plant oils examined its fatty acid profile for cosmetic use.[9] The seed oil study in keratinocytes and fibroblasts examined whether the oil protected skin cells from UV-induced changes, in cell culture only.[11]
Wikipedia and general reference accounts do not give safety information for the oil; it is used as a food colourant and supplement as well as a cosmetic ingredient.[2][7]

A double-blind randomised trial of 86 completers examined 2 g daily of oral sea buckthorn oil for three months against placebo in people with dry eye, assessing tear osmolarity and symptoms; its title reports that the oil attenuated tear film osmolarity and symptoms.[14] A companion trial examined oral sea buckthorn oil's effects on tear film fatty acids in dry eye.[21]

Registered trials on ClinicalTrials.gov include oral and topical treatment for skin aging (n=60, status unknown), effects on mucous membranes (n=116), dry eye (n=100), and eye health with lutein.[5][6][15][16] A flavonol-focused human study examined absorption and cardiovascular risk markers using sea buckthorn products, and a randomised crossover trial in overweight women examined sea buckthorn and bilberry effects on serum metabolites.[13][22] A 2024 in vitro study examined the oil's effect on muscle precursor cell proliferation.[23] No published results of the skin-aging trial and no controlled published trial on facial appearance were found.

timeline.event: Tibetan medical text Somaratsa is reported to describe use of the fruit and oil.[2]
Soviet researchers are reported to study the oil in skincare and nutrition programmes.[2]
Trials on oral and topical oil for skin aging and for dry eye are registered.[5][6]
A randomised trial reports effects of oral oil on tear film osmolarity in dry eye.[14]

Moisturising and antioxidant support for skin
angle.text: Sea buckthorn oil is applied in creams and oils, or taken as a supplement, with the aim of hydrating skin and giving it a healthier, more even look. Appearance claims rest on its composition and laboratory findings.
